header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's stoa0180a.stoa005.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's CSEL (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0180a.stoa005.opp-l: Letter 1: 'te' in 'inuadente (te)' is an editorial supplement. Simon is taken to be Simon Magus; Valens is probably the Arian-party bishop of Mursa. Letter 2: 'u' in 'interim u distrahit' is read as 'me'. Letter 4: the opening is syntactically difficult; 'his formanda' (perhaps 'his informanda') is translated by sense. 'i defendere' is uncertain and may be corrupt, as the object of 'defend' is unclear; 'he' in the last sentence is presumably the emperor. Letter 5: 'semis' read as 'seruis', 'solarium' as 'solacium', 'regant' as 'rogant'. Letter 6: 'monebat' read as 'mouebat'; 'dignam' as 'dignum'; 'locatus' as 'locutus'; 'sanctas' as 'sanctus'; 'intellectas' as 'intellectus'; 'hob' as 'hoc'. 'aK here' is garbled, probably 'aliquid' or 'alicubi'. In 'testis est autem 547q quia', '547' is treated as a page mark and the subject of 'testis est' as truth, which is uncertain because a word such as 'deus' may be lost. 'crura agunt' is read as 'curam agunt'; if taken literally it would refer to harm to legs. 'donec morte am sui Pharaenis' is damaged: 'am' is left untranslated, and the sense 'by the death of their Pharaoh' is tentative. 'merit. home ... farnule' read as 'merito homo ... famule'.

7.2: 'neg(otia)' is the edition's expansion; the clause on 'those who ought to marvel at our reverence towards God' is obscure. 7.3: the sentence beginning 'quasi illas litteras' has no main verb in the text, so '[I had suppressed]' is supplied from context. 'si deo fidem debet' ('if he owes faith to God') looks like an oath-like aside but is obscure. 7.4: 'horam' is read as 'horum', 'exhibitis' as 'exhibiti', and 'significant' (of Alexander) as 'significat'; the construction 'horum si fas est sententiis quale sit aut quid habeat commodare consensum' is awkward and the rendering is approximate. 7.5: 'tegatorum' is read as 'legatorum'. The final sentence is difficult: 'an' seems to require a lost alternative or a different reading, possibly 'whether the cause of a man should be treated rather than the law of religion preserved'. 7.6: 'cum exemplo' is suspect and may be corrupt; the syntax of this long sentence is loose. 8.ab2: 'BOBOBATIS' is read as 'roboratis'; the wording 'to those devoted... and to the most beloved brothers' may refer to one group. 8.1: 'et a nobis reuertentes' is translated as printed, though 'as if coming to you and returning from us' may mean that they falsely claim to come from Athanasius. 'indiscretum' is taken as 'a matter of indifference', and could also mean 'that there is no distinction'.

nodes.text: VI. LETTERS OF LUCIFER AND OF OTHERS.
I. LETTER OF LUCIFER, PANCRATIUS AND HILARY TO BISHOP EUSEBIUS.
To the most honourable lord Bishop Eusebius, Bishop Lucifer, the priest Pancratius, and Hilary.

Now that the devil's head and his wicked promptings have been trampled underfoot, holy lord, we ask you not to neglect the grace granted you by our Lord, but be pleased to hasten now, so that as you press the attack the doctrine of the Arians may be put to flight as quickly as possible. For the Lord and his Christ know that, just as at the coming of the most blessed apostles the name of God was glorified in the ruin of Simon, so, with Valens driven out at your coming, the machinery of the blaspheming Arians may be dismantled and destroyed. We, most holy lord, from the first day we came to Vercelli until today, long for your Reverence and ask the Lord that all the saints may praise a lasting restoration in this church and honour your spiritual power with the praise it is owed. We believe that this will come about, because we are confident that the Saviour's passion cannot be overcome. May Christ the Lord keep you glorious, most holy and most blessed one.
II. LETTER OF POPE LIBERIUS TO LUCIFER, WHILE IN EXILE.
Bishop Liberius to his most beloved brother Lucifer.

Although under the appearance of peace the enemy of the human race seems to have raged more violently against the members of the Church, yet your excellent and singular faith shows you, priests most acceptable in the Lord, to be approved by God here too, and has already marked you out as martyrs for the glory to come. And so with what proclamation of praise, with what exultation of voice, may I set forth the merits of your virtue? Placed as I am between grief at your absence and joy at your glory, I simply cannot find a way, except that I know I offer you more acceptable comfort if you believe that I have been thrust into exile together with you. Indeed, I am much saddened that, while I am still left hanging in this very expectation, a harsher necessity keeps me for the present apart from your company. For I had wished, most devoted brothers, to be spent first on behalf of all, so that your Charity might rather follow the example of glory through me. But let this be the palm of your merits, that you have been first to come, through perseverance in the faith, to the illustrious glory of confession. I therefore beg your Charity to believe that I am present with you, and to feel that in affection I am not absent, and to understand that I grieve greatly at being for the present separated from your company. How great a glory you have attained, you can know all the better from this: whereas those crowned in persecution could feel only the bloody swords of the persecutor, you, soldiers of God devoted in all things, have also experienced false brothers as enemies and have carried off the victory over faithlessness; and the more their violence has been able to grow in this world, the more they are found to confer rewards of praise on the holy priests. Be therefore secure in the heavenly promise, and since you have been brought nearer to God, lift me up to the Lord by your prayers, me your fellow priest and servant of God, so that we may be able to bear with endurance the assaults that come upon us, which day by day inflict heavier wounds as they are reported, and that, with the faith inviolate and the Catholic Church's standing safe, the Lord may deign to make me equal to you. And because I wish to know more reliably what was done in that very conflict, I implore your Holiness to be pleased to report everything faithfully by letter, so that both my mind, which is tormented by conflicting rumours, and the strength of my body, which is already worn down, may feel greater increase from your encouragement. [And in another hand:] May God keep you safe, lord brothers.
III. LETTER OF FLORENTIUS TO LUCIFER.
To the most kind lord Lucifer, Florentius.

A certain person has presented a book in your name to our lord and Augustus; he has ordered it to be brought to your Holiness and wishes to learn whether this same book was sent by you. You must therefore write down what is true, in good faith, and send the book back, so that it may be presented once again to his Eternity.
IIII. LETTER OF LUCIFER TO FLORENTIUS.
To Florentius, master of offices, Bishop Lucifer.

Your religious prudence was to be informed of these things, dearest son: that the bearer of the book, who your Honour says approached the emperor in my name, was sent by my humble self, and also that the book itself, as you were pleased to direct, was carefully examined and handed over to Bonosus, *agens in rebus* [an imperial agent], to be carried back. It will now be for your nobility to defend without any hesitation [what has been] acknowledged by me. For he will find us, by God's favour, standing glad against what is being prepared for our death, when he begins to examine the reasons why I wrote in such a manner.
V. LETTER OF ATHANASIUS TO LUCIFER.
To the most beloved lord and brother Lucifer, bishop and confessor, Athanasius, greeting in the Lord.

Being by God's favour well in body, we have sent even now our dearest Eutyches the deacon, so that your religious Holiness also may be pleased to inform us, as we hope and desire, of your safety and that of all your people. For we believe that through you, confessors and living servants of God, the state of the Catholic Church is being renewed, and that what the heretics have tried to tear apart our Lord Jesus Christ is restoring to wholeness through you. For although the forerunners of Antichrist have done everything through the power of this world to put out the lamp of truth, yet the Godhead through your confession has shown its light the brighter, so that their deceit can be hidden from no one. Before now they could at least pretend; now they are called antichrists. For who would not curse them? Who would not flee their communion as a stain and a serpent's venom? Every church everywhere mourns, every city groans, aged bishops toil in exile, and the heretics pretend not to notice, who by denying Christ have made themselves tax-collectors, sitting in the churches and exacting revenues. O new kind of men and of persecution, which the devil has invented, that he should use such ministers for wrongdoing and with so much cruelty! But even if they do such great things and have extended their arrogance and blasphemies, yet your confession, piety and wisdom are no small but a very great comfort and a great consolation to the brotherhood. For it has reached us that your Holiness has written to Augustus Constantius, and we marvel more and more that, dwelling as if in the midst of scorpions, you nevertheless use your freedom of spirit, so that by warning or teaching or correcting you may lead those who go astray to the light of truth. I ask therefore, and all the confessors ask with me, that you be pleased to send us a copy, so that all may perceive not only by hearsay but also from the writing itself the virtue of your soul and the confidence and freedom of your faith. Those who are with me greet your Holiness; I greet all who are with you. May the Godhead always keep you safe, vigorous and mindful of us, most beloved lord and truly man of God.
VI. LETTER OF ATHANASIUS TO LUCIFER.
To the most glorious lord and deservedly most longed-for fellow bishop Lucifer, Athanasius, greeting in the Lord.

Although I believe that word has reached your Holiness too of the persecution which even now the enemies of Christ have attempted against the brotherhood, seeking our blood, yet our dearest brothers can also report it to your Reverence; for they have dared to extend their rage through soldiers so far that they not only drove out the clergy of the city but even went out into the deserts and laid their deadly hands on the monks. So it came about that I too withdrew further away, so that those who had taken us in might not also suffer trouble from the same men. For whom will the Arians spare, who have not spared their own souls? And when can they turn back from their abominable deeds, while they persist in denying the Lord Christ, the only Son of God? This is the root of their depravity; on this sandy foundation of theirs they build their perverse ways, as we find written in the thirteenth psalm: The fool said in his heart: there is no God; and soon there follows: They have been corrupted and have become abominable in their works. For this reason the Jews, denying the Son of God, deserved to hear: Woe, sinful nation, people full of offences, evil seed, children without law. Why without law? Because you have forsaken the Lord. For this reason the most blessed Paul, when he had begun not only to believe in the Son of God but also to preach his Godhead, wrote: I am conscious of no evil in anything. So, in keeping with your confession, we too desire, holding the apostolic tradition, to live according to the commandments of the divine law, so that we may be found with you in that choir in which patriarchs, prophets, apostles and martyrs now rejoice. Although, then, the Arian madness was so stirring itself up with outside power that the brothers were not permitted even to look freely upon the air, so fiercely were they raging, yet according to your prayers, by God's favour, though with toil and danger, I was able to see the brother who is accustomed to send necessities as well as letters, both from your Holiness and from others. So we received the letters and books of your most religious and most wise soul, in which we beheld the image of an apostle, the confidence of a prophet, the teaching authority of truth, the doctrine of the true faith, the heavenly way, the glory of martyrdom, triumphs over the Arian heresy, the unimpaired tradition of our fathers, the right rule of ecclesiastical order. O truly Lucifer, who, according to your name, bearing the light of truth, have set it on a lampstand so that it may shine for all! For who, except the Arians, does not see clearly from your teaching the true faith and the stain of the Arians? Greatly and wonderfully, as light is [separated] from darkness, so you have separated truth from the cunning and hypocrisy of the heretics, you have defended the Catholic Church, you have proved the Arians' words to be nothing but mere fantasy, you have taught that the devil's gnashings are to be trampled underfoot. How good and delightful are your exhortations to martyrdom, how supremely desirable you have shown death for Christ the Son of God to be, what love of the world to come and of heavenly life you have made manifest! You seem to be a true temple of the Saviour, who, dwelling in you, himself says these things through you, he who has given such grace to your words; for you were lovable to all even before, but now so great a love of affection for you is placed in the hearts of all that they call you the Elijah of our times. And no wonder; for if those who seem to please God are called sons of God, how much more fitting is it to call confessors above all sharers with the prophets. Believe me, Lucifer, you alone have not spoken these things, but the Holy Spirit with you. From where comes so great a memory of the scriptures, from where an unimpaired sense and understanding of them? From where such a composed order of speech? From where such exhortations to the heavenly way? From where the confidence against the devil and the proofs against the heretics, unless the Holy Spirit had been placed in you? Rejoice therefore, seeing clearly that you are already in that place where your predecessors the martyrs also now are, that is, in the choir of angels. We too rejoice, having in you an example of virtue, patience and freedom. As for what you have written about my name, I blush to say anything, lest I seem a flatterer; but I know and believe that the Lord himself, who revealed all knowledge to your holy and religious soul, will repay you for this labour also with a reward in the kingdom of heaven. Since, then, you are such a man, we ask you to be an intercessor for us through prayers to the Lord, that he, merciful as he is, may now deign to look upon the Catholic Church and rescue all his servants from the hands of the persecutors, so that all those too who have fallen through fear of the moment may at last be able to raise themselves and return to the way of righteousness, from which they wander led astray, wretched men, not knowing in what pit they are. But I ask especially that, if anything has been said by me inadequately, you be pleased to forgive it; for from so great a spring my lack of skill has scarcely managed to draw what it could. As for our brothers, if I have been less able to see them, again I ask you to forgive me. For truth itself is witness that I wished and desired to obtain this and felt great grief that I could not; for neither have the tears ceased from my eyes nor the groans from my soul, because we are not permitted even to see the brothers. It is witness too that I have not been able to see even the kinsfolk I have, from the time they began to persecute us. For what do the Arians not do? They watch the roads, they keep a lookout on those setting out and leaving the city, they search ships, they circle the deserts, they disturb houses, they harass the brothers, they contrive trouble for each one; but thanks be to God, while they do these things, they are all the more cursed by everyone and are recognised, truly, as your Holiness has said, as slaves of Antichrist; and the wretches, while they are held in hatred, persist in their malice until, by the death of their Pharaoh, they too are condemned. Those who are with me greet your Reverence; be pleased to greet those who are with you. May the divine grace of God keep you safe, mindful of us, ever blessed, deservedly man of God, servant of Christ, sharer with the apostles, comfort of the brotherhood, teacher of truth, and in all things most longed-for.
VII. LETTER OF LIBERIUS.
To the most glorious Constantius Augustus, Bishop Liberius.

I desire, most tranquil emperor, that your Clemency grant me kindly ears, so that I may be able to lay open the purpose of my mind to your Gentleness. For from a Christian emperor and a son of Constantine of holy memory I ought to deserve to obtain this very thing without delay; but I understand that I am struggling in this, that by repeated self-justification I cannot call back into favour towards me your spirit, which is placable even towards the guilty. For the speech of your Piety, sent some time ago to the people, tears me deeply, I who must bear all things patiently; but that your spirit, which is ever given to mildness, which never, as it is written, keeps its anger until the going down of the day, should retain its indignation against me is a marvel to me. For I, most religious emperor, seek with you a true peace, one not composed in words with an inward arrangement of deceit, but reasonably established on the precepts of the Gospels. Not only the business of Athanasius but many other matters have come into the open, on account of which I had begged your Gentleness that a council be held, so that before all else, as the sincere devotion of your mind towards God especially desires, when the cause of the faith, in which our first hope towards God lies, had been diligently treated, the affairs of those who ought to marvel at our reverence towards God could be settled. And it would have been worthy of a worshipper of God, worthy of your rule, which is governed and increased by the piety of Christ, that your Clemency should grant us this very thing, especially out of reverence for the holy religion to which you are prudently attentive, for obtaining these things.

But many hasten to tear the members of the Church, who have invented the story that I suppressed letters, so that the crimes of the man whom they were said to have condemned should not be open to all, as though [I had suppressed] those letters of the Eastern and Egyptian bishops in which the same crimes against Athanasius were contained throughout. But it is clear enough to everyone, and no one denies it, that we made known the letters of the Easterners, that we read [them] to the church, read [them] to a council, and moreover replied to the Easterners on these matters, to whom we did not lend our faith and judgement, because at the same time the judgement of seventy-five Egyptian bishops concerning Athanasius stood against [them], which we likewise read aloud and made known to the Italian bishops. Hence it seemed to be against the divine law, since the number of bishops in favour of Athanasius was greater, to lend consent in any part. These writings, if he owes faith to God, Theosebius, who had been sent and was hastening to Africa, left with us; all of which writings, however, so that they should not be lacking perhaps for obtaining a council, Vincentius, who had been sent with the others as a legate, afterwards brought to Arles.

Your Prudence therefore sees that nothing has entered my mind which it was unworthy for those who serve God to think. God is my witness, and witness is the whole Church with its members, that by faith and fear towards my God I trample and have trampled upon all worldly things, as the rule of the Gospels and the apostles has commanded; not with reckless fury, but living by the divine law established and observed, and in my other ecclesiastical ministry I fulfilled nothing that pertained to the law through boastfulness, nothing through desire of glory; and I came to this office, God my witness, unwillingly, in which I desire indeed to remain without offence to God as long as I am in the world, and I have ensured that never my own statutes but the apostolic ones should always be upheld and guarded. Following the custom and order of our forebears, I have added nothing to the episcopate of the city of Rome and have allowed nothing to be diminished, and keeping that faith which has run down through the succession of so many bishops, of whom many were martyrs, I earnestly desire that it always be guarded unimpaired. Lastly, ecclesiastical concern and devotion itself persuade me now to lay open my case to your Piety. The Easterners indicate that they wish to be joined in peace with us. What peace is this, most clement emperor, when there are from those very parts four bishops, Demophilus, Macedonius, Eudoxius, Martyrius, who eight years ago at Milan, when they refused to condemn the heretical opinion of Arius, walked out of the council with angry spirits? Your Equity and Clemency will be able to judge whether it is right to lend consent to the judgements of these men, and of what sort it is and what it entails. What is now being attempted subtly and under the pretext of the name of Athanasius is nothing new. There remain letters of Bishop Alexander, sent long ago to Silvester of holy memory, in which he indicates that before the ordination of Athanasius he expelled from the church eleven, priests as well as deacons, because they followed the heresy of Arius, some of whom, now placed outside the catholic Church, are said to have found conventicles for themselves, with which Georgius in Alexandria is also affirmed to be in communion by letter. What peace, then, can there be, most tranquil emperor, if bishops, hauled in as has now been done throughout Italy, are forced to obey the judgements of such men?

Hear another thing, since your Tranquillity patiently allows it. There remain the letters of the legates who had been sent to your Clemency, which came recently, in which they indicate that on account of the disturbance of all the churches they had indeed been willing at first to submit to the judgements of the Easterners, but that they had set a condition, that if these same men condemned the heresy of Arius, they would on these terms be inclined to obey their judgements. The agreement, as they themselves indicate, is confirmed by written testimony. They go into the council; they receive, after deliberation, the replies that they could not condemn the doctrine of Arius, [but that] Athanasius, which was all they demanded, must be deprived of communion. From this let your Clemency also now consider whether, with the law of the catholic religion rightly preserved, the cause of a man ought to be treated diligently and searchingly.

Therefore again and again I ask your Gentleness, your spirit devoted to God, by the power of him who has shown all mortals how great he is in your defence, having before your eyes the benefits of him who rules your empire in all things, see that these matters are diligently treated in an assembly of bishops with all consideration, so that, the times having been pacified through you with God's favour, and with your Tranquillity consenting, all things may be so examined that what has been confirmed by the judgement of the priests of God, once it is established that all have agreed, all together, in the exposition of the faith which was confirmed among so many bishops at Nicaea in the presence of your father of holy memory, may be kept with [that] example for the future, so that the Saviour himself, who looks down from above on the purpose of your mind, may rejoice in so great a settlement of affairs, that you have not undeservedly set the cause of faith and peace before even the necessities of the state. To entreat your Gentleness, then, that you may deign to hear our representations with a kindly spirit, it was resolved that my brother and fellow bishop, the holy man Lucifer, should set out with Pancratius my fellow presbyter and Hilary the deacon, who we believe can without difficulty obtain from your Clemency a council for the peace of all the catholic churches. May the clemency of Almighty God guard you for us, most clement and most religious Augustus.
VIII. LETTER OF ATHANASIUS.
Athanasius, to those devoted to the solitary life and strengthened in the faith of God, and to the most beloved brothers, greeting in the Lord.

I give thanks to the Lord, who has granted you to believe in him, so that you too may have eternal life with the saints. But since there are some who hold the opinions of Arius, going around the monasteries for no other purpose than to seduce the simple, as if coming to you and returning from us, and there are some who affirm that they do not hold the opinions of Arius but go and pray together with them, at the urging of the most sincere brothers I have of necessity taken care to write, so that, keeping sincerely and without guile the pious faith which the grace of God works in us, you may not give occasion of scandal to the brothers; for when someone sees you, the faithful in Christ, in communion with such men or praying together with them, they surely, thinking this a matter of indifference, fall into the mire of impiety. So that nothing of the kind may happen, let it be your care, dearest brothers, to turn away those who hold the opinions of the Arian impiety, and to shun those who are thought not to hold the opinions of Arius but who pray with the impious, especially because it is fitting to flee also the communion of those whose thinking we curse. If anyone comes to you, then, and if, according to blessed John, he brings the right doctrine, say to him "Hail" and receive such a man as a brother; but if anyone pretends to confess the right faith but appears to be in communion with them, urge a man of this kind to abstain from such association, and if he promises, regard him too as a brother. But if he persists with a contentious spirit, avoid him as well. It was possible for me to extend this letter at length as well, setting out from the divine Scriptures the pattern of this kind of doctrine, but because, being prudent, you anticipate those who write, and being more intent upon abstinence are fit also to teach others, I have therefore dictated briefly, as one who loves to those who love, confident that, living in this way, you will keep a pure and sincere faith, and that those men, seeing now that you do not pray together with them, will gain benefit from it, fearing that they may be reckoned as impious and as those who hold the opinions of those men.
